entry.title: Draft a GitHub pull request in Claude Code with a /pr slash command
entry.summary:
If you keep pasting the branch diff and "write a PR title and body, then wait" into Claude Code, turn that prompt into a slash command. The file name becomes the command; $ARGUMENTS lets you name the base branch or add extra instructions. Save this as .claude/commands/pr.md: --- description: "Draft a GitHub pull request from the current branch" argument-hint: "[base branch | extra instructions]" ---
Draft a GitHub pull request for the current branch. Do not create it until I confirm.
1. Run `git status -sb`, `git log --oneline -15`, and `git diff origin/HEAD...HEAD` (or `main...HEAD` if `origin/HEAD` is missing). If there is no unique commit versus the base, stop and say so. 2. If I passed arguments (`$ARGUMENTS`), treat the first token as a base branch when it looks like one (`main`, `master`, `develop`, or `origin/...`). Treat the rest as extra instructions. 3. Propose a PR title and a body with a short summary, a test plan, and any follow-ups. Do not add AI attribution unless I ask. 4. Show the title and body and wait for me to confirm before running `gh pr create`. Never force-push, never merge, and never add reviewers I did not name.
Use it as /pr, /pr main, or /pr develop include a migration note. Slash commands are markdown files in .claude/commands. Claude Code injects the file as the prompt and replaces $ARGUMENTS with whatever you type after the command. Keeping "wait for confirm" and "never force-push or merge" in the command reduces unattended PR creation. Pair this with an "ask" permission rule for gh pr create if you also want a permissions bump. Commit the command file so every teammate gets the same workflow. Pair with a /commit command so the branch messages and the PR body stay consistent. I keep copy-ready Claude Code configs (CLAUDE.md templates, slash commands, hooks, permission rules) in Vildanden Agent Config. There's a free sample: https://justly-mia-429.rehost.page/

entry.title: How to Schedule Daily Email Reports: Reliable Webhook Fan-Out
entry.summary: A daily report is not a cron-expression problem. It is a delivery contract: start the work once, tell many subscribers about the same shipment state, and make a retry harmless. For a healthtech system, that contract matters more than shaving a few lines from the scheduler configuration. Short answer: schedule a public Node.js webhook to enqueue the report, keep the webhook short, and let a worker send email tasks idempotently. Treat the scheduler as a trigger, not as the place where the report is rendered. This design fits a daily email report when the work can be handed off quickly; a workflow engine is a better boundary for long-running dependencies or joins. Infrai fits the trigger-and-handoff slice when one REST interface and one key reduce integration friction across backend services.…

entry.summary: AI coding assistants can generate an Android screen, connect an API, and produce a working APK surprisingly quickly. But a working APK is not the same as a secure application.
